text:
Question 1
Import and load the apdc_firstcvd. Determine the age and sex of each patient, reducing to one observation per ppn that was most frequently reported for the index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease.


Show R code
# Retrieve age and sex from apdc_firstcvd
age_sex <- apdc_firstcvd %>% select(ppn, age_recode, sex)

# Count observations per person
age_sex <- age_sex %>% group_by(ppn) %>% 
            mutate(rn = row_number()) %>% 
            ungroup()

#Reshape to cross check discrepancies
age_sex_wide <- age_sex |> pivot_wider(
  id_cols=ppn,
  names_from = rn, 
  values_from = c(age_recode, sex)
)

#Compare for discrepancies - for age
age_sex_wide %>% mutate(flag_age = case_when(
                        is.na(age_recode_2) ~ 0,
                        age_recode_1 != age_recode_2 & is.na(age_recode_3) ~ 1,
                        (age_recode_1 != age_recode_2 | age_recode_1 != age_recode_3) & is.na(age_recode_4) ~ 1,
                        (age_recode_1 != age_recode_2 | age_recode_1 != age_recode_3 | age_recode_1 != age_recode_4) & is.na(age_recode_5) ~ 1,
                        (age_recode_1 != age_recode_2 | age_recode_1 != age_recode_3 | age_recode_1 != age_recode_4 | age_recode_1 != age_recode_5) ~ 1,
                        TRUE ~ 0
                        )
                     ) %>% 
  filter(flag_age==1) %>%  print()


# A tibble: 1 × 12
  ppn     age_recode_1 age_recode_2 age_recode_3 age_recode_4 age_recode_5 sex_1
  <chr>          <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl>        <dbl> <dbl>
1 T1ckqS…           54           54           55           NA           NA     2
# ℹ 5 more variables: sex_2 <dbl>, sex_3 <dbl>, sex_4 <dbl>, sex_5 <dbl>,
#   flag_age <dbl>


Show R code
#Compare for discrepancies - for sex
age_sex_wide %>% mutate(flag_sex = case_when(
                        is.na(sex_2) ~ 0,
                        sex_1 != sex_2 & is.na(sex_3) ~ 1,
                        (sex_1 != sex_2 | sex_1 != sex_3) & is.na(sex_4) ~ 1,
                        (sex_1 != sex_2 | sex_1 != sex_3 | sex_1 != sex_4) & is.na(sex_5) ~ 1,
                        (sex_1 != sex_2 | sex_1 != sex_3 | sex_1 != sex_4 | sex_1 != sex_5) ~ 1,
                        TRUE ~ 0
                        )
                     ) %>% 
  filter(flag_sex==1) %>%  print()


# A tibble: 0 × 12
# ℹ 12 variables: ppn <chr>, age_recode_1 <dbl>, age_recode_2 <dbl>,
#   age_recode_3 <dbl>, age_recode_4 <dbl>, age_recode_5 <dbl>, sex_1 <dbl>,
#   sex_2 <dbl>, sex_3 <dbl>, sex_4 <dbl>, sex_5 <dbl>, flag_sex <dbl>


There is only one discrepancy for age and none for sex. Looking at PPN “T1ckqS0bQ2Q”, there were two occurrence of age 54 and one occurrence of age 55. This is plausible to have occurred if the patient had their birthday during their hospital admission. Regardless, we will take the most frequently reported value of age 54.



Show R code
# Reduce age and sex to one value per ppn
age_sex_ppn <- age_sex_wide %>% select(ppn, age_recode = age_recode_1, sex = sex_1)

title: Module 5 Solutions
text:
Question 3
Using the apdc_subset, we will calculate a Charlson comorbidity index (CCI) for each patient with a 1 year lookback period. Complete the following to create a dataset with one row per patient and their corresponding CCI. This will also be used to derive whether they have diabetes and diabetes complications.

Create a new dataset, apdc_subset_com, that restricts the dataset to the index hospital admission and any episodes of care within 1 year prior to the index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease.



Show R code
# Episodes of care for index hospitalisations & 1 year prior
apdc_subset_com <- analysis_data_v2 %>% 
            select(ppn, sepdate_last) %>% 
            right_join(apdc_subset, by = "ppn") %>% 
            filter((sepdate_last-episode_end_date)>=0 & (sepdate_last-episode_end_date)<=365.25) 



Create new variables for each of the comorbid condition that flag whether that condition was ever recorded during each episode of care.

We will be using the charlson() function, so we need to add decimals to the diagnosis code variables.



Show R code
## Load charlson package
library(devtools)
install_github("james-hedley/charlson")
library(charlson)

# Charlson package codings
comorbidity::available_algorithms()


Supported comorbidity mapping algorithms:
    * charlson_icd9_quan 
    * charlson_icd10_quan 
    * charlson_icd10_se 
    * charlson_icd10_am 
    * charlson_icd10_am_ucodes 
    * elixhauser_icd9_quan 
    * elixhauser_icd10_quan 

Supported scoring weights algorithms:
    * For charlson_icd9_quan: charlson, quan 
    * For charlson_icd10_quan: charlson, quan 
    * For charlson_icd10_se: charlson, quan 
    * For charlson_icd10_am: charlson, quan 
    * For charlson_icd10_am_ucodes: charlson, quan 
    * For elixhauser_icd9_quan: vw, swiss 
    * For elixhauser_icd10_quan: vw, swiss 


Show R code
# Add decimal to diagnosis variables
dcodes <- c(paste0('diagnosis_code',c('P',seq(1:19))))

for (v in dcodes) {
  apdc_subset_com[[v]] <- ifelse(
    is.na(apdc_subset_com[[v]]),
    NA,
    paste0(substr(apdc_subset_com[[v]], 1, 3), ".", substr(apdc_subset_com[[v]], 4, nchar(apdc_subset_com[[v]])))
  )
}

# Create cogrp based on each episode of care (to create separate flags for each condition)
apdc_subset_com <- apdc_subset_com %>%
  charlson(newvar = cogrp,
           diagnosis_code_vars = paste0('diagnosis_code',c('P',seq(1:19))))



Collate the multiple lines per ppn for the comorbid conditions across the episodes of care, into one line per ppn.



Show R code
# Update flags if patient has record of condition during index admission or previous 12 months
flag_vars <- c("ami", "chf", "pvd", "cva", "dementia", "pulmonary_disease",
               "ctd", "peptic_ulcer", "liver_disease", "diabetes",
               "diabetes_complications", "paraplegia", "renal_disease",
               "cancer", "metastatic_cancer", "severe_liver_disease", "hiv")

#Create comorbidity flags
apdc_subset_com <- apdc_subset_com %>%
  group_by(ppn) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(flag_vars), ~ max(replace_na(.x, 0)))) %>%
  ungroup()



Calculate the CCI manually and name the variable cogrp. We would like you to exclude the following comorbidities from your CCI: any cardiovascular comorbidities (including myocardial infarction mi, congestive heart failure chf, peripheral vascular disease pvd, cerebral vascular accident cva), renal disease rend and, diabetes diab and diabetes complications diabwc (for further evaluation) from the final calculation. Merge this into your analysis dataset, analysis_data_v2.



Show R code
# Manually calculate Charlson comorbidity index for each patient
apdc_subset_com <- apdc_subset_com %>%
  mutate(cogrp = 
           ami * 0 + #Exclude myocardiacl infarction
           chf * 0 + #Exclude congestive heart failure
           pvd * 0 + #Exclude peripheral vascular disease
           cva * 0 + #Exclude cerebral vascular accident
           dementia * 1 +
           pulmonary_disease * 1 +
           ctd * 1 +
           peptic_ulcer * 1 +
           liver_disease * 1 +
           diabetes * 0 + # Exclude diabetes
           diabetes_complications * 0 + # Exclude diabetes complications
           paraplegia * 2 +
           renal_disease * 0 + # Exclude renal disease
           cancer * 2 +
           metastatic_cancer * 6 +
           severe_liver_disease * 3 +
           hiv * 6)

# Add cogrp back to analysis dataset
analysis_data_v2 <- apdc_subset_com %>% 
          select(ppn, cogrp) %>% 
          distinct() %>% 
          right_join(analysis_data_v2, by = "ppn")

  tabyl(cogrp)

  pull(cogrp) %>%

                                  margin = margin(r = 10)),

        axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"),

title: Module 5 Solutions
text:
Question 5
We will now be determining if patients had procedures CABG (codes 38497, 38500, 38503, 90201) or PCI (codes 35310, 35304-00, 30305-00). However, the procedure is not necessarily captured during the index admission but generally within 30 days of index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease.

Using the apdc_subset, create a new dataset apdc_subset_proc. Flag all episodes of care that involved a CABG or PCI procedure, regardless of whether this was before or after the index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease.



Show R code
# Create procedure flags
procedure_vars <- paste0("procedure_code", c("P", seq(1, 19)))

#Create copy of dataset
apdc_subset_proc <- apdc_subset %>% 
  # Flag each episode of care as containing CABG or PCI
  mutate(cabg = if_any(all_of(procedure_vars), ~ str_sub(.x, 1, 5) %in% c("38497", "38500", "38503", "90201")) * 1,
         pci = case_when(
           if_any(all_of(procedure_vars), ~ str_sub(.x, 1, 5) %in% c("35310")) ~ 1,
           if_any(all_of(procedure_vars), ~ .x %in% c("35304-00", "30305-00")) ~ 1,
           TRUE ~ 0))



Calculate the time variable (time_proc) that is the time between an episode of care with CABG or PCI procedure and the index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease. First, merge in the index hospital admission date from analysis_data_v2 into apdc_subset_proc and then calculate the time variable.



Show R code
#Merge in index hospital admission
apdc_subset_proc <- analysis_data_v2 %>%

TipOPTIONAL



Instead of copy-pasting the same code and changing a variable name each time, we can create a function that produces the plot we want. See below R coding and example.




Show R code
# Nicer plots -  if interested
kmplot <- function(variable) {
  ## If variable is not already a factor, convert it to one
  data <- analysis_data_v2
  data[variable] <- as.factor(data %>% pull(all_of(variable)))
  
  ## Calculate p-value using log-rank test
  pval <- survdiff(data = data,
                   formula = as.formula(paste0("Surv(time = survtime, event = status) ~ ", variable)))$pvalue
  
  ## Format p-value
  pval_label <- case_when(
    pval >= 0.9 ~ "p = 0.9",
    pval >= 0.095 ~ paste0("p = ", round(pval, 1)),
    pval >= 0.0095 ~ paste0("p = ", round(pval, 2)),
    pval > 0.001 ~ paste0("p = ", round(pval, 3)),
    TRUE ~ "p < 0.001")
  
  ## Create survfit object for KM plot
  survfit <- survfit(data = data,
                     as.formula(paste0("Surv(time = survtime, event = status) ~ ", variable)))
  
  ## Create vector of factor levels
  factor_levels <- data %>% pull(all_of(variable)) %>% levels()
  
  ## Create dataset for plotting
  plotdata <- tidy(survfit) %>%
    select(strata, time, estimate) %>%
    mutate(strata = factor(
      str_replace(strata, ".*=", ""),
      levels = factor_levels)) %>%
    bind_rows(tibble(strata = factor(factor_levels, levels = factor_levels), 
                     time = 0, 
                     estimate = 1), .) %>%
    arrange(strata, time, estimate) %>% 
    filter(time<=10)
  
  ## Create KM plot
  plot <- ggplot(data = plotdata, mapping = aes(x = time, y = estimate)) +
    geom_line(aes(colour = strata, linetype = strata), linewidth = 1) +
    geom_point(data = plotdata %>% 
                 mutate(year = floor(time)) %>%
                 group_by(strata, year) %>%
                 slice(1) %>%
                 ungroup(),
               aes(colour = strata, shape = strata),
               size = 2) +
    annotate(geom = "text", x = 10, y = 0.95, label = paste0("Log-rank ", pval_label),
             size = 4, colour = "black", hjust = 1) +
    xlab("Years since ACS admission") +
    ylab("Proportion alive (%)") +
    labs(colour = variable, linetype = variable, shape = variable) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10),
                    ylim = c(0, 1),
                    clip = "off") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10,
                       minor_breaks = seq(0, 10, 1/12),
                       expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25),
                       labels = seq(0, 100, 25),
                       minor_breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05),
                       expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text = element_text(colour = "black", size = 11), 
          axis.title = element_text(colour = "black", size = 14, face = "bold"), 
          axis.line = element_line(colour = "black"),
          axis.ticks = element_line(colour = "black"),
          legend.position = "right",
          legend.key.width = unit(1, "cm"),
          legend.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
          panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "grey95", linewidth = 0.7),
          panel.grid.minor = element_line(colour = "grey98", linewidth = 0.2),
          panel.border = element_blank(),
          plot.margin = margin(t = 10, b = 10, l = 10, r = 10))
    
  ## Return KM plot as output
  return(plot)
}

Calculate adjusted Charlson comorbidity index
Now we can use these hospital admissions to calculate the Charlson comorbidity index (CCI)
First we use the charlson() function to create flags for each comorbidity used in the CCI, by checking all the diagnosis code variables from diag1-diag51


Show R code
cci_adj <- apdc_2yrpreKRT %>%
  charlson(diagnosis_code_vars = paste0("diag", seq(1:51)))


For each comorbidity, we can check whether it was EVER flagged in any hospital admission. To do this, we collapse our dataset down to one row per person (PPN), and replace each flag with its maximum value (within each person). It will be easier if we first create a character vector with the names of all the comorbidity flags

                 "diabetes", "diabetes_complications", "paraplegia", 
                 "renal_disease", "cancer", "metastatic_cancer", "hiv")

  group_by(ppn) %>%
  summarise(across(comorb_vars, ~ max(.x)))

Determine remoteness of each SA2
Now we need to look up the remoteness classification for each person’s SA2 code in anzdata_patients. The SA2 codes provided are based on the 2016 census. Also, our cohort includes people with kidney failure from 2015-2019, so using remoteness classifications from 2016 is also appropriate (since this will be at most 3 years different from kidney failure date, and remoteness classifications don’t shift that much in only 3 years).
We can find the relevant mapping between 2016 SA2 codes and 2016 remoteness areas (RA) here: https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/asgs-geographic-correspondences-2016
Download the zip file, and find the relevant excel fill within it “CG_SA2_2016_RA_2016.xlsx”. You can also download it here. Save this to our data_dir, so we can read it in here. Before we read it in, open this file in Excel and determine where the data we need is located. In this case it is on worksheet “Table 3”, in cells A6:F2602.

CG_SA2_2016_RA_2016 <- read_excel(path = file.path(data_dir, paste0("CG_SA2_2016_RA_2016", ".xlsx")),

Note there are some SA2 codes that appear in multiple rows. This happens when an SA2 region lies partially in one remoteness area, and partially in another. You can investigate this yourself here: https://maps.abs.gov.au/
The first SA2 in our dataset, Braidwood, is one example. It lies partially in ‘Inner Regional Australia’ and partially in ‘Outer Regional Australia’. The PERCENTAGE column shows what proportion of the population of this SA2 lives within each remoteness area.
For our analysis, we need to assign a single remoteness level to each SA2, so we need to make an assumption. One option is to assume the most urban classification. Another option could be to assume the least urban classification. The option we’ll use here is to determine the median classification, i.e. for each SA2, in which remotness area does the 50th centile person live.

text:
Question 7
Define how you would appropriately construct a study population with all the available hospitalisation data to determine length of stay for their kidney transplant admission. Consider what records should be included. What important assumptions have we made in constructing this study population?
Steps for constructing the study population:
1. Determine which episodes of care were part of the same hospital admission.
2. Flag any hospital admissions where any diagnosis code within any episode of care was related to kidney transplant
3. Remove episodes of care if there was no kidney transplant flagged for the entire hospital admission.
4. Calculate length of stay for each hospital admission (latest episode end date minus earliest episode start date).
5. Collapse the dataset to one row per person per kidney transplant hospital admission, keeping the length of stay for each admission.
Assumptions:
1. Hospital admissions are for kidney transplant even if the primary diagnosis code was unrelated.
2. We are assuming the entire length of stay was attributable to the kidney transplant, and not other medical issues that arose.
3. All transfers have been accounted for correctly, and there were no interstate transfers.

text:
Question 9
Define the data processing steps that would be necessary to identify and group together the episodes of care to reflect the same hospitalisation admission.

If an episode of care is nested within another episode of care, it must be part of the same admission. We would take the earliest episode start date and latest episode end date to define the admission
If an episode starts on the same day that another ends, we would need to check the mode of separation, as well as the facility code, facility transferred from, and facility transferred to. Then we can determine which episode end date would be most appropriate
If an episode of care does not have overlapping dates with another episode of care, they are two separate admissions and each episode start date and end date can be used respectively.

title: Module 2 Exercises
text:
Context
Kidney transplantation is the most compelling treatment option for kidney failure, conferring both survival and quality of life benefits. A kidney can be donated from either a living donor or a deceased donor. Once a kidney transplant fails, people may go on to receive another kidney transplant. Some patients also require a liver transplant, either concurrently or at a different time to kidney transplantation. This exercise will give you the opportunity to explore kidney transplantation in administrative health data.
Please note that while these are real data of real individuals, you have been provided with a perturbed selection and so estimates are not reflective of true transplantation rates.

title: Module 2 Exercises
text:
PART ONE
Patient demographics are collected across several administrative health datasets. We have provided age and sex from redacted data across several health administrative databases. Use these data to make comparisons within and across datasets to decide upon the most appropriate value to use for each patient.
canc_reg.csv – Cancer registry, includes age and sex at cancer diagnosis, and date of cancer diagnosis.
napd.csv – Non-admitted patient data, includes age and sex at date of outpatient service, and date of outpatient service.
pbs.csv – Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, includes age and sex at date of dispensing medication, and date of dispensing medication.
dth.csv – Deaths records, includes age and sex at date of death, and date of death.
anzdata.csv – Australian and New Zealand Dialysis and Transplant Registry data, includes age and sex at date of receiving dialysis or transplant, and date of dialysis or transplant.

title: Module 2 Exercises
text:
Question 1
Import kidney_long.csv and save into data frame (kidney_long). Familiarize yourself with the data items.
The file includes kidney transplant recipients and the date and donor type of their respective kidney transplants. Some people may receive multiple kidney transplants over their lifetime.
Create a tx_seq sequence variable that counts each kidney transplant for each patient.
How many people in the dataset received 2 or more kidney transplants?

title: Module 2 Exercises
text:
Question 2
Now write and run the code to create an “index_seq” variable (call this variable post_ltx_seq) on the end of each record to flag for living donor transplants. Assign a value of 1 for the first record where the kidney transplant was from a living donor (using the donortype variable) and then count any subsequent kidney transplants. This variable flags the first living donor kidney transplant and counts all subsequent kidney transplants regardless of the type of donor (i.e. living or deceased donor).

How many patients had at least one kidney transplant from a living donor?
How many patients with a living kidney donor transplant had at least one subsequent kidney transplant?

title: Module 2 Exercises
text:
Question 3
For patients who had another kidney transplant after their living donor transplant, most will have a deceased donor transplant but some may have another living donor transplant. Write and run the code that creates a variable liv_seq (living donor transplant sequence) on the end of each record. This assigns the value of 1 for the index record (first living donor transplant) and increments each time a subsequent transplant is from a living donor.

What is maximum number of living donor transplants to one patient in our study population?
How many patients had at least one additional living donor transplant after their first living donor transplant?

Your sequence numbering should look like the following output. Note the difference between the post_ltq_seq and liv_seq. We suggest you check your coding using the patient with ID “P9119912”.

title: Module 2 Exercises
text:
Question 4
For the below questions, we want to look at the donor type of subsequent kidney transplants following a living donor transplant.







CautionHint





Remind yourself of what the post_ltx_seq variable represents and restrict the records you will look at using the post_ltx_seq variable



We want to determine whether having a living donor kidney transplant, either as the first kidney transplant or subsequent kidney transplant, influences the donor type of their next kidney transplant (if any). That is, does the proportion of patients whose next kidney transplant is from a living donor differ depending on whether their first kidney transplant was a living donor or a deceased donor?
Now, remembering that the post_ltx_seq variable counts from the first living donor transplant (which may not be the first kidney transplant for the patient as they may have had prior kidney transplants) and tx_seq variable counts all their kidney transplants. Using post_ltx_seq and tx_seq appropriately:

Determine what proportion of patients had a deceased donor transplant immediately following their first living donor transplant.
Determine what proportion of patients had a deceased donor transplant immediately following their first living donor transplant, where their first living donor transplant was also their first ever kidney transplant.
Determine what proportion of patients had a deceased donor transplant following their first living donor transplant which was NOT their first kidney transplant.

Merge datasets


Show R code
merged_data <- left_join(anzdata_patients_clean, 
                         anzdata_transplants_clean,
                         by = "ppn")


left_join since we want to keep all of the records in anzdata_patients, and look up their corresponding transplant information from anzdata_transplants
Since some people can have more than one transplant, this is a 1-to-many merge. Each PPN appears exactly once in the left-hand dataset (anzdata_patients). But each PPN can potentially appear more than once (many times) in the right-hand dataset (anzdata_transplants)
The merged dataset will therefore contain multiple rows per person, one row for each transplant

This would be somewhat expected if we are back-calculating from the age in years. We do not have a decimal for age in years to indicate how far along in the age of year the individual is, that is someone who has had their birthday in May being 34 years would be the same age in years even until the following April. This would not be the case if we had a decimal for the age in years.

Considering this, let’s remove month of birthdate as we rarely would expect this to match between different dates. We will then collapse down to one year of birthdate - simply taking the first year of birth date.

Question 4
Recall that we have already applied the transfers code transfers() in case any transfers occurred during the first kidney transplant and to ensure we captured the correct subsequent hospital admissions. However, as we then kept only hospital admissions following the first kidney transplant, several of the newly created variables would not technically still be correct.
fileseq would not be correct as we removed observations. episode and stayseq may be correct in certain circumstances (i.e. if their first hospital admission for the data period was the first kidney transplant) but generally would not always - although it is consecutively correct, it would not always start from 1 for the first observation for a patient. transfer, transseq, admdate_first, sepdate_last and totlos would all be correct.
Keeping this in mind, let’s start by reducing our dataset to the necessary variables (i.e. ppn, stayseq, admdate_first, sepdate_last, totlos and cvd_flag) and removing duplicates.Consider any additional data checks you may need to undertake to ensure the resulting dataset has one row per ppn per hospital admission. Then, we will recreate fileseq and create an index sequence varaible (index_seq) to flag the first admission with cardiovascular disease (if any) for each patient using the cvd_flag.


Show R code

  select(ppn, stayseq, admdate_first, sepdate_last, totlos, cvd_flag) %>%

Then, create a separate flag variable for each of the following types of inconsistency and report the total number of cases where these occurred:


Show R code

# Check for inconsistencies with death dates 
  # a) Mode of separation is death with autopsy, but death date is missing
  mutate(dodgy_flag_a = (mode_of_separation_recode == "6" & is.na(death_date)) * 1) %>%
  # b) Mode of separation is death without autopsy, but death date is missing
  mutate(dodgy_flag_b = (mode_of_separation_recode == "7" & is.na(death_date)) * 1) %>%
  # c) Date of death is before admission

  # d) Date of death is more than 1 day before separation

  group_by(dodgy_flag_a, dodgy_flag_b, dodgy_flag_c, dodgy_flag_d) %>%
  summarise(n = n()) %>%

  arrange(any_dodgy_flag, desc(dodgy_flag_a), desc(dodgy_flag_b), desc(dodgy_flag_c), dodgy_flag_d) %>%

Context
The aim of this exercise is to examine how the survival of people hospitalised with cardiovascular disease following their first kidney transplant varies by remoteness (ARIA) and socioeconomic status (SEIFA), accounting for important confounders and procedure performed (if any). We will create additional variables for inclusion as potential covariates.
We wish to include or create the following variables:

Age
Sex
Remoteness
Socioeconomic status
Diabetes and diabetes complications
Other comorbidity
Procedures performed (i.e. CABG and/or PCI)

Recall that we included:
ICD diagnosis codes: The ICD-10-AM codes for cardiovascular disease included I20-I25, I34-I37, I42, I44-I49, I60-I61, and I63.
The diagnosis codes are stored in the character variables (diagnosis_codeP, diagnosis_code1 to diagnosis_code39), allowing up to 40 diagnoses during one admission.
ICD procedure codes: The ICD-10-AM codes for the relevant revascularisation procedures are: 38497, 38500, 38503, 90201 are the codes for coronary artery bypass grafts (CABG); 35310, 35304-00, 30305-00 are the codes for percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), including angioplasty with or without stents.
The procedure codes are stored in the character variables (procedure_codeP, procedure_code1 to procedure_code49), allowing up to 50 procedures during one admission.
Note, our APDC dataset was trimmed to only include up to 20 diagnoses and 20 procedures per admission.

For the Index of Relative Socio-economic Disadvantage, decile one is interpreted as being most disadvantaged, and decile ten is least disadvantaged.


```{r}
## Read in csv file
seifa_sa2_mapping <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NicoleDeLaMata/LinkedData/refs/heads/main/seifa_sa2_mapping_2016.csv")
```

title: Module 5 Exercises

Question 3
Using the apdc_subset, we will calculate a Charlson comorbidity index (CCI) for each patient with a 1 year lookback period. Complete the following to create a dataset with one row per patient and their corresponding CCI. This will also be used to derive whether they have diabetes and diabetes complications.

Create a new dataset, apdc_subset_com, that restricts the dataset to the index hospital admission and any episodes of care within 1 year prior to the index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease.
Create new variables for each of the comorbid condition that flag whether that condition was ever recorded during each episode of care.







CautionHint





The provided charlson() function also calculates flags for each condition, so you can use this to help you develop your coding. However, you must ensure the diagnosis codes contain a decimal after the third character (i.e. E101 must be E10.1). Fix this first before running the charlson() function.




Collate the multiple lines per ppn for the comorbid conditions across the episodes of care, into one line per ppn.







CautionHint





Take the maximum value for each comorbid condition flag per ppn.




Calculate the CCI manually and name the variable cogrp. We would like you to exclude the following comorbidities from your CCI: any cardiovascular comorbidities (including myocardial infarction mi, congestive heart failure chf, peripheral vascular disease pvd, cerebral vascular accident cva), renal disease rend and, diabetes diab and diabetes complications diabwc (for further evaluation) from the final calculation. Merge this into your analysis dataset, analysis_data_v2.
Examine the frequency distribution of cogrp.
Convert cogrp to a categorical variable with categories: 0, 1, 2 and 3+ and tabulate this variable.

Question 5
We will now be determining if patients had procedures CABG (codes 38497, 38500, 38503, 90201) or PCI (codes 35310, 35304-00, 30305-00). However, the procedure is not necessarily captured during the index admission but generally within 30 days of index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease.

Using the apdc_subset, create a new dataset apdc_subset_proc. Flag all episodes of care that involved a CABG or PCI procedure, regardless of whether this was before or after the index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease.
Calculate the time variable (time_proc) that is the time between an episode of care with CABG or PCI procedure and the index hospital admission for cardiovascular disease. First, merge in the index hospital admission date from analysis_data_v2 into apdc_subset_proc and then calculate the time variable.
Create two separate histograms of the time variable for those with CABG and those with PCI. Comment on the distribution.
Reduce the dataset apdc_subset_proc to one observation per ppn, ensuring you obtain data on the CABG or PCI performed in closest date proximity to the index hospital admission (i.e. the observation with the lowest absolute time in time_proc). Merge the flag and time for CABG and PCI into the analysis_data_v2.
How many patients had a CABG or PCI or both?
What proportion of patients had a CABG procedure prior to or within 30 days after the index hospital admission? Similarly, what proportion of patients had a PCI procedure prior to or within 30 days after the index hospital admission?
Where procedures were conducted more than 30 days, set the cabg or pci to 0.
